title: SWOT analysis is usually credited to Harvard Business School's planning course, or to Albert Humphre
description:
SWOT analysis is usually credited to Harvard Business School's planning course, or to Albert Humphrey inventing it alone at Stanford. A 2023 peer-reviewed history in the journal Long Range Planning found that neither claim holds up.

Led the long-range planning group at the Stanford Research Institute where the framework was actually built, and first called it SOFT, not SWOT.

SOFT stood for Satisfactory, Opportunity, Fault, Threat: the present and future of an organisation, sorted into what was working and what was not. Albert Humphrey worked on the same SRI team. He relabelled it SWOT, for Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, Threats, in a paper he published in 1974.

The Harvard Business School origin story does not hold up either. William Guth, the last surviving member of Harvard's 1960s policy faculty, said in 2017 he was confident no one on that faculty created the framework.

A tool built to help you check your assumptions had one about its own history.

Sources:
- https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0024630123000110 - Puyt, Lie and Wilderom's 2023 peer-reviewed history in the journal Long Range Planning traces SWOT's real origin to Robert F. Stewart's Theory and Practice of Planning group at the Stanford Research Institute, active between 1962 and 1971; states Stewart developed the SOFT approach (Satisfactory, Opportunities, Faults, Threats) in 1965, calling it 'the progenitor of SWOT analysis in all its variations'; records that SOFT was later relabelled Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, Threats by Albert Humphrey, a member of the same SRI team, in his 1974 publication 'Getting management commitment to planning'; and quotes William D. Guth, the last surviving Harvard Business School policy faculty member from the 1960s, saying in 2017 he was confident no one on that faculty created the framework, against the popular claim that it originated there.
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_S._Humphrey - confirms Humphrey worked on a team led by Robert Stewart that published the SOFT framework at the Stanford Research Institute, distinguishing his role in relabelling the tool from Stewart's role in creating it.
